unit.title: Bubbles and crises
unit.description: From tulips to FTX: what happened in each crisis and what rules it left us
unit.section: A history of crises and bubbles

u34l1.title: Tulips and the South Sea Company

steps.title: Tulip mania
steps.body:
In the Dutch Republic (today's Netherlands), in the winter of 1636-1637, bulbs of rare tulips reached crazy prices: some sold for the price of a house. In February 1637 the buyers vanished and prices collapsed.

Historians argue about how many people were really ruined, but it's the classic example of a bubble.

steps.title: The South Sea, 1720
steps.body:
The South Sea Company promised riches from trade with South America. In 1720 its shares went from about 128 pounds in January to over 1,000 in the summer… and by the end of the year they were back at January levels.

Isaac Newton sold at a profit, bought back in near the top and lost about 20,000 pounds. He's credited with saying: «I can calculate the motion of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people».

steps.title: The eternal pattern
steps.body: A real or promised novelty → rising prices → people buying just because it's rising → easy credit → «this time it's different» → nobody else buys → a rapid fall.
steps.key: Bubbles change their costume, but they follow the same script.
steps.tip: When you buy something only because you think someone else will pay you more for it, you're already inside a bubble.

steps.title: The Roaring Twenties
steps.body:
In the '20s the US stock market went through a period of euphoria: radio, cars, electricity… Lots of people bought shares **on credit**: they put in around 10 % and the broker lent them the rest.

The Dow Jones peaked on 3 September 1929. In October came **Black Thursday** (the 24th) and **Black Tuesday** (the 29th).

steps.title: The fall
steps.body:
With borrowed money, a 10 % drop already wiped out all your money, and brokers forced people to sell. Forced selling fuelled further falls.

By July 1932, the S&P 500 had fallen **83 %** and the Dow Jones 89 %. The Great Depression had arrived.

steps.title: How long did it take to recover?
steps.body: The Dow Jones didn't get back to its 1929 peak until **1954**: about 25 years, not counting dividends. With dividends, and taking into account that prices fell (deflation), about 15 years. People with no debts could wait; those who'd bought on credit couldn't.
steps.key: Leverage turns a fall into ruin.

steps.title: The internet was changing everything
steps.body:
In the late '90s, any company with «.com» in its name shot up on the stock market, even if it didn't make any money. IPOs that doubled in price on the first day, valuations in the billions without any profits.

The Nasdaq peaked on 10 March 2000, above 5,000 points.

steps.title: The fall
steps.body:
By October 2002, the Nasdaq had fallen nearly **78 %**. Pets.com went public in February 2000 and shut down that same November. Amazon fell more than 90 %… and survived.

The Nasdaq took about **15 years**, until 2015, to get back to its peak.

steps.title: The lesson
steps.body: The internet really did change the world: the idea was good. The problem was the **price**. A great company can be a bad investment if you pay too much for it.
steps.key: Price matters: being right about a technology isn't enough to make money.

steps.title: Mortgages that couldn't be repaid
steps.body:
In the US, millions of **subprime mortgages** were handed out: loans to people with little ability to repay. Banks bundled them into securities (**securitisation**) that rating agencies rated as very safe, and they were sold all over the world.

When house prices fell, defaults soared.

steps.title: Lehman Brothers
steps.body:
Banks were heavily indebted and held those securities on their balance sheets. On 15 September 2008 **Lehman Brothers**, one of the big US investment banks, went bust. Panic spread and credit froze.

From its October 2007 peak, the S&P 500 fell as much as **57 %**.

steps.title: The lesson
steps.body: Even the «experts», the banks and the rating agencies got it wrong. Keep an emergency fund so you don't have to sell at the worst moment, and avoid products you don't understand.
steps.key: If you don't understand how a product works, you don't know what risk you're taking.

steps.title: The great Japanese bubble
steps.body:
In the '80s, Japan was the economy everyone was talking about. Shares and land shot up on cheap credit and sky-high valuations. Japan became the **largest stock market in the world**.

The Nikkei 225 closed at **38,915 points** on 29 December 1989.

steps.title: The lost decade… and more
steps.body:
Then came years of falls and stagnation. In March 2009 the Nikkei got as low as about **7,055 points**, 82 % below its peak.

It didn't top 38,915 points again until **February 2024: 34 years later**.

steps.title: The lesson
steps.body: A whole country, rich and advanced, can go decades without getting back to its peak. That's why «the stock market always recovers» is only true with time, diversification and no debt. A global index doesn't depend on any one country doing well.
steps.key: Diversify across countries: even the world's largest stock market can stagnate for 30 years.

u34l6.title: Spain: the housing bubble and the risk premium

steps.title: Bricks and mortar
steps.body:
Between the late '90s and 2007, Spain went through a **housing bubble**: hundreds of thousands of homes were built every year, on easy credit, and many savings banks (cajas) lent far too much to property.

The IBEX 35 peaked in November 2007, close to 15,950 points. Then came the 2008 crisis… and in Spain, a second one.

steps.title: The risk premium
steps.body:
The **risk premium** is the difference between what the Spanish 10-year bond pays and what the German one pays. 100 basis points = 1 %.

In July 2012 it went above **600 points**: the Spanish bond was paying over 7 %. In June, the Eurogroup had approved up to €100,000 million to clean up the banks, and the IBEX fell below 6,000 points.

steps.title: The turning point
steps.body: On 26 July 2012, Mario Draghi, President of the ECB, said he would do «whatever it takes» to save the euro. People who only held Spanish shares suffered far more than those diversified around the world.
steps.key: Your own country can have its crisis too: diversifying across countries isn't just for other people.

steps.title: The fastest fall
steps.body:
On 19 February 2020 the S&P 500 hit a peak. The pandemic shut down half the world and by 23 March it had fallen **34 %**: in just **33 days**.

Central banks and governments responded with huge stimulus.

steps.title: The fastest recovery
steps.body:
By 18 August 2020, the S&P 500 was already back at its peak: about **5 months** later.

Anyone who sold in March «to wait until things became clearer» missed a big chunk of the rebound. According to J.P. Morgan, 7 of the 10 best days of 2005-2024 came within two weeks of one of the 10 worst.

steps.title: The lesson
steps.body: Nobody called the 23 March bottom in advance. What worked was the boring stuff: not panic selling, keeping up contributions and rebalancing.
steps.key: Nobody can predict the bottom: panic selling was the big mistake of 2020.
steps.tip: Time in the market beats timing the market.

steps.title: From euphoria to winter
steps.body:
Bitcoin hit nearly **$69,000** in November 2021 and dropped to about **$15,500** in November 2022: −77 %. Many other cryptos fell more than 90 %.

Remember: crypto is very volatile, it isn't regulated like a deposit and **you can lose everything you've invested**.

steps.title: Terra and FTX
steps.body:
• **May 2022, Terra:** its algorithmic «stablecoin» UST lost its peg to the dollar. Its platform offered about 20 % a year, «stable». Within days, Terra and its LUNA coin lost almost all their value: around 40,000 million dollars.
• Platforms like Celsius froze withdrawals and went bust.
• **November 2022, FTX:** one of the biggest exchanges collapsed after using its customers' money. Its founder was sentenced to 25 years in prison.

steps.title: The lesson
steps.body: A «stable» 20 % return is a sign of risk, not of safety. An exchange isn't a bank with a deposit guarantee scheme: if it goes bust, your crypto can get trapped. That's why people say «not your keys, not your coins».
steps.key: In crypto, the risk isn't just the price: it's also who's holding your money.

u34l9.title: What all crises have in common

steps.title: The same script
steps.body:
Tulips, 1929, 2000, 2008, crypto… Almost every time you see:

• An exciting **novelty**.
• Easy **credit** or leverage.
• **Euphoria**: «this time it's different».
• A burst and **panic**.
• A recovery… for those who could wait.

steps.title: The five rules
steps.body:
1. Don't invest with borrowed money.
2. Diversify across companies, sectors and countries.
3. Keep an emergency fund so you never have to sell.
4. Don't pay any price.
5. Don't panic sell: if your plan is a 20-year one, a fall lasting months doesn't change it.
steps.key: Those who were diversified, debt-free and patient recovered from every crisis.
steps.tip: Crises don't give warning, but you can prepare for them.

u34l1-1.prompt: Put the typical stages of a bubble in order.
options: Prices rise and attract more buyers
The first ones sell and buyers stop coming in
Euphoria: people buy just because it's rising, often on credit
u34l1-1.explanation: It's the pattern described by economists like Kindleberger and Minsky: it repeats century after century.

u34l1-2.prompt: Where and when did tulip mania happen?
options: In the Dutch Republic (the Netherlands), around 1637
u34l1-2.explanation: London 1720 is the South Sea Company.

u34l1-3.prompt: What happened to Isaac Newton with the South Sea Company?
options: He made a fortune and retired
He sold at a profit, bought back in at a higher price and lost about 20,000 pounds
u34l1-3.explanation: Not even one of the most brilliant minds in history escaped the euphoria.

u34l1-4.prompt: Historians argue about how far tulip mania really ruined lots of people.
u34l1-4.explanation: Some studies think the impact was smaller than the legend says, but the price pattern really did happen.

u34l1-5.prompt: You're in London in the summer of 1720. Your South Sea shares have gone up eightfold in six months. A friend says: «This time it's different, trade with the Americas has no limit». What do you do?
options: Buy more with a loan: it just keeps going up
Convince my whole family to get in
Take some of the profits and be wary of «this time it's different»
u34l1-5.explanation: «This time it's different» is the most expensive phrase in the history of markets.
feedback: Buying with debt at the height of euphoria is a recipe for ruin. By the end of the year the shares were back at January levels.
That's how the last stage of a bubble works: the latecomers pile in.
Sensible: when the price drifts that far from the real business, the fall is usually just as fast.

u34l1-6.prompt: Match each bubble with the promise that fuelled it.
u34l1-6.explanation: The product changes; the psychology is the same.

u34l1-7.prompt: The phrase that pops up in almost every bubble is «this time it's ____».
u34l1-7.explanation: Every generation believes its novelty breaks the rules.

u34l1-8.prompt: Quick: buying something only because you think someone else will pay you more for it is called…
u34l1-8.explanation: It works until there's nobody left willing to pay more.

u34l1-9.prompt: Sign of a bubble or of a healthy market?
options: People taking out loans to get in
«This time it's different, the old rules don't apply»
A reasonable valuation relative to what the company earns
Everyone's talking about it, even people who've never invested
The price rises in line with profits
u34l1-9.explanation: Euphoria, credit and ignoring valuations are the classic alarm bells.

u34l1-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: If my hairdresser is making money, it must be easy
Then I'm getting in now, before it's too late!
When everyone's talking about something, it's usually a sign of euphoria, not opportunity
u34l1-10.explanation: Widespread euphoria is an alarm bell, not an invitation.
feedback: Something having gone up doesn't make it easy or safe.
When even people who never invest are in, who's left to buy?
Well spotted! It's been one of the classic signs of a bubble since 1637.
lines: My neighbour bought a car with what he made on a new coin 🤑
And my hairdresser's got in too!

u34l2-3.explanation: From that peak began one of the biggest falls in stock market history.

u34l2-4.prompt: In the '20s, many people bought shares by putting in 10 % and borrowing the rest. What did that mean?
options: That a 10 % fall could wipe out all their money
That the bank took on the losses
That they couldn't lose more than 10 %
u34l2-4.explanation: With 10-to-1 leverage, a −10 % move in the price is a −100 % hit to your money.

u34l2-5.prompt: You put in €1,000 and borrow €9,000 to buy €10,000 of shares. They fall 10 %. After paying back the loan, how much do you have left?
u34l2-5.explanation: The shares are worth €9,000, exactly what you owe. Your €1,000 has vanished with just a −10 % move.

u34l2-6.prompt: The Dow Jones took about 25 years to get back to its 1929 peak, not counting dividends.
u34l2-6.explanation: It didn't beat it until 1954. With dividends and deflation, the real recovery was shorter, about 15 years.

u34l2-7.prompt: The S&P 500 fell 83 % between 1929 and 1932. How much did it then have to rise to get back to its peak? (round it)

options: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday, in October 1929
The Dow gets back to its peak in 1954
Euphoria of the '20s and buying on credit
u34l2-8.explanation: The rise took years; the fall, just a few; the recovery, decades without dividends.

u34l2-9.prompt: Quick: what's the big lesson of the 1929 crash?
options: You should only invest in one country
Leverage turns a fall into ruin
u34l2-9.explanation: Without debt you could wait; with debt, you were forced to sell at the worst moment.

u34l2-10.prompt: It's 1930. The stock market has fallen 40 %. Ana owes nothing and won't need the money for years. Bruno bought on credit and his broker is asking for more collateral. Who has more options?
options: Ana: with no debt, nobody can force her to sell
Both the same: it's the same stock market
Bruno, because if he puts in more money he can recover more
u34l2-10.explanation: Not investing with borrowed money is the first rule history teaches us.
feedback: Exactly. Time is only on your side if you can wait.
Same market, opposite situations: debt decides who can hold on.
Bruno has to put in money he may not have or sell at the worst moment. And there was still more to fall.

u34l3-1.prompt: This is how the Nasdaq 100 moved between late 1997 and March 2000. What trend do you see? (Nasdaq 100 · weekly closes · to 06/03/2000)
u34l3-1.explanation: It more than quadrupled in just over two years: enthusiasm for the internet seemed to have no ceiling.

u34l3-2.prompt: It's 6 March 2000. The Nasdaq 100 has more than quadrupled in two years thanks to the internet. What did it do over the next two and a half years?
u34l3-2.explanation: The internet really did change the world; the question was whether those prices already priced in all that future and more.
u34l3-2.horizon: the next two and a half years

u34l3-3.prompt: March 2000: you have 100 % of your savings in tech funds, which have risen 300 % in three years. Your brother-in-law tells you to sell «even just a bit». What do you do?
options: Take out a loan to buy more
Nothing: the internet is the future
Go back to a diversified mix: less tech and some bonds
u34l3-3.explanation: Diversifying and rebalancing protect you from bubbles without having to guess when they'll burst.
feedback: Debt, concentration and sky-high prices: the most dangerous combination.
The internet was the future, and even so the Nasdaq fell nearly 78 % and took 15 years to recover.
Sensible: you don't need to guess the top, just not depend on a single expensive sector.

u34l3-4.prompt: How long did the Nasdaq take to get back to its March 2000 peak?

u34l3-5.prompt: The Nasdaq fell nearly 78 %. How much did it have to rise to get back to its peak? (round it)

u34l3-6.prompt: Amazon fell more than 90 % after the dot-com bubble and still survived.
u34l3-6.explanation: A great company can also be a bad investment for years if you buy it too expensively.

u34l3-7.prompt: What became of these dot-com era companies?
u34l3-7.explanation: Pets.com shut down in 2000 and Webvan went bust in 2001. Picking the survivors in advance was almost impossible: another reason to diversify.

u34l3-8.prompt: A great company is always a good investment, whatever you pay for it.
u34l3-8.explanation: The price you pay to get in decides a big part of your return.

u34l3-9.prompt: What signs of a bubble were there in 1999-2000? Select all that apply.
options: Lots of new people buying just because it was rising
IPOs that doubled in price on the first day
Companies with no profits valued in the billions
u34l3-9.explanation: Valuations were forgotten: «the old rules don't apply any more».

u34l3-10.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes, just like the internet in 2000
The technology can be real and the price can still be too high
u34l3-10.explanation: Being right about a technology doesn't guarantee being right about the investment.
feedback: In 2000 the internet did change everything… and the Nasdaq fell 78 %.
You don't need to decide whether it's a fad: just don't pay any price and diversify.
That's it! What matters isn't just the idea, but how much you pay for it.

options: House prices fall and defaults rise
Heavily indebted banks pile up losses
They're bundled into highly rated securities and sold around the world
Lehman Brothers goes bust and panic breaks out
Mortgages are given to people who could hardly afford them
u34l4-1.explanation: A chain in which each link amplified the one before.

u34l4-2.explanation: At that point nobody knew whether the worst was over: the chart only shows the past.

u34l4-3.prompt: It's 2 March 2009. The S&P 500 has fallen more than 50 % and the headlines are talking about a new Great Depression. What did it do over the following months?
u34l4-3.explanation: At that point fear was everywhere and nobody knew whether the fall was over.

options: Mortgages for people with little ability to repay

u34l4-6.prompt: March 2009: your portfolio has fallen 45 % and you won't need the money for 20 years. Your plan says «I don't sell during a fall». What do you do?
options: Move everything into gold for good
Stick to the plan, keep contributing and rebalance if needed
Sell everything, this has no bottom
u34l4-6.explanation: With an emergency fund and no debt, a fall doesn't force you to sell.

Selling in March 2009 meant selling near the bottom: what came next was one of the biggest rallies in history.

u34l4-7.prompt: Rating agencies gave very high grades to mortgage securities that later collapsed.
u34l4-7.explanation: That's why «very safe» in a brochure is no substitute for understanding what you're buying.

u34l4-8.explanation: 1 ÷ 0.43 − 1 ≈ 1.33 → +133 %. With dividends, the S&P 500 took about 4 years to get back to its peak.

u34l4-9.prompt: Quick: what lesson does 2008 leave for an individual investor?
options: Keep an emergency fund and avoid products you don't understand
u34l4-9.explanation: Even the big banks got it wrong about what was on their own balance sheets.
